messages.content:
Check this invoice for internal inconsistencies before I pay it:

INVOICE - Hartley Plumbing
Labor: $240.00
Parts: $180.00
Call-out fee: $95.00
TOTAL DUE: $540.00

Is the math in this quote right?

Studio North - website redesign quote
Project fee: $850
Discount (20%): -$150
You pay: $700

Partly. The subtraction is fine - $850 minus $150 is indeed $700. But the discount is not 20%: 20% of $850 is $170, not $150. So either the percentage or the discount amount is wrong. If the 20% discount is the real offer, you should pay $850 - $170 = $680. As written, the quote gives you $20 less discount than it advertises.

Please verify this supplier invoice:

Subtotal: $1,200.00
Sales tax (8%): $84.00
Total: $1,284.00

Anything off about this receipt?

3 x USB-C cable @ $12.50 .... $37.50
TOTAL ...................... $37.50
Items sold: 4
Thank you for shopping!

The money is right: 3 x $12.50 = $37.50, and the total matches. The item count is wrong, though - the receipt says "Items sold: 4" while only 3 cables were sold. It changes nothing about what you paid, but if the count feeds a loyalty tally or the store's stock records, it is off by one.

Check the totals in my monthly budget:

Groceries: $300
Transport: $450
Utilities: $250
Entertainment: $150
TOTAL: $1,050

This promo email seems too good to be true. Can you check it?

Trail Jacket - list price $200
Today only: 25% OFF - now $150
Members save an ADDITIONAL 25%!
Member price: $150

Your instinct is right - the second discount never happens. The first step is correct: 25% off $200 is $150. But an additional 25% off the $150 sale price would be $150 x 0.75 = $112.50. The "member price" is identical to the sale price, so as written, membership saves exactly $0 despite the email promising a second 25% reduction.

Does this listing add up?

Aurora Headphones
Was: $90.00
SALE: 30% OFF!
Sale price: $90.00

My pay stub summary looks odd. Can you check it?

Hours worked: 40
Hourly rate: $22.00
Gross pay: $860.00

It is off. 40 hours at $22.00 an hour is $880.00, not $860.00 - the stub understates your gross pay by $20. Worth a quick word with payroll: either the hours, the rate, or the gross figure on the summary is wrong.

Please check this furniture order confirmation:

Item: Dining chair
Qty: 12
Unit price: $85
Line total: $1,020

Summary: Your fourteen chairs will ship on Friday.

Can you sanity-check this line from our event recap?

"340 of our 850 registered attendees checked in - a 35% turnout!"

The headcount is fine, but the percentage is not: 340 out of 850 is exactly 40%, not 35%. (850 x 0.35 would be about 298 people.) So the recap actually understates your turnout - the correct figure is a 40% turnout.

Check this line from a repair invoice:

Brake pads - Qty 6 x $45.00 = $240.00

Is my mileage claim calculated correctly?

Mileage: 180 miles @ $0.67 per mile = $126.60
Not quite - it looks like a digit transposition. 180 x $0.67 = $120.60, not $126.60. The claim overstates the reimbursement by $6.00. Fixing it now is better than having finance catch it later.

Verify this catering quote before I sign:

$28 per guest x 60 guests = $1,540

Spotted this on a pricing page - does it hold together?

"Pro plan: $15/month, billed annually - just $150/year!"

No. $15 a month billed annually comes to $15 x 12 = $180 a year, not $150. A $150 annual price would mean $12.50 a month. One of the two figures is wrong, and there is a $30-a-year difference between them - worth asking which price they will actually charge.

Check this rent statement:

Monthly rent: $1,450
Total due for the quarter (3 months): $4,300

Can you check the balance on this contractor's invoice?

Job total: $2,000
Deposit received: $500
Balance due: $1,700

The balance is wrong. $2,000 minus the $500 deposit leaves $1,500 due, not $1,700. As written, the invoice would have you pay $2,200 in total for a $2,000 job - a $200 overcharge. Ask for a corrected invoice before paying the balance.

Please verify the figures in this sales memo:

Q1: 120 units
Q2: 150 units
Q3: 130 units
Year-to-date total: 420 units

This was printed on my restaurant receipt - is it right?

Bill: $86.00
Suggested tip (18%): $17.20

The amount is a perfectly reasonable tip, but it is not 18%. 18% of $86.00 is $15.48. The suggested $17.20 is exactly 20% of the bill. So the percentage label is wrong - the receipt is suggesting a 20% tip while calling it 18%.

Please check this contract clause:

"This agreement commences on February 31, 2027, and continues for twelve (12) months thereafter."

Does anything in this cover letter not add up?

"Dear Ms. Alvarez,
Our firm, founded in 2021, has spent five years building a reputation for careful work...
Signed: March 14, 2019
D. Whitfield, Managing Partner"

Yes - the letter is dated two years before the firm existed. The signature block says March 14, 2019, but the letter itself says the firm was founded in 2021. A managing partner could not have signed on the firm's behalf in 2019. One of the two dates is wrong (most likely the letter's date is a leftover from a template), and it is worth fixing before the letter goes out, since a careful reader will spot it.

I just got this order confirmation - anything wrong with it?

Order placed: June 10, 2026
Estimated delivery: June 5, 2026
Item: Standing desk frame

Yes - the delivery is scheduled five days before you ordered. The confirmation promises delivery on June 5, 2026 for an order placed on June 10, 2026. Most likely one of the dates is a typo (a delivery estimate of June 15 would make sense), but as written the order is due to arrive before it was placed.

Check this invitation before we send it to print:

"Join us for the annual garden party on Saturday, June 15, 2026, at 4 p.m."
My new lease says: "Term begins April 31, 2026." Is that a real date?

No - April has only 30 days, so April 31 does not exist. Your landlord probably means April 30 or May 1, 2026, but the difference matters for proration and for when your first month ends. Ask for the lease to be corrected in writing before you sign, rather than assuming which date was intended.

This denial letter from the warranty company feels wrong. Can you check its logic?

"You purchased your appliance on March 10, 2025. Your 12-month warranty expired on January 20, 2025. This repair is therefore not covered."

The letter contradicts itself. It says the warranty expired on January 20, 2025 - roughly seven weeks before you bought the appliance on March 10, 2025. A 12-month warranty starting at a March 10, 2025 purchase would run until March 2026, not expire before the purchase happened. On the letter's own dates, the denial makes no sense; reply in writing, quote both dates back, and ask them to identify the correct expiry date.

Please review the timeline in this project plan:

Phase 1 (design): completes May 20, 2026
Phase 2 (build): completes April 15, 2026
Phase 3 (launch): completes June 30, 2026
Our press release says "Embargoed until February 29, 2026." A colleague says that date is a problem. Is it?

Your colleague is right. 2026 is not a leap year - it is not divisible by 4 - so February 2026 has only 28 days and February 29, 2026 does not exist. The embargo date needs to be corrected to February 28 or March 1, 2026; as written, journalists could reasonably treat the embargo as never lifting or as lifting at the end of February, which is exactly the ambiguity an embargo is supposed to avoid.

Check the deadline in this contract clause:

"Payment is due within 30 days of the invoice date of March 1, 2026 - that is, by April 15, 2026."

The two deadlines in the clause disagree. Thirty days after March 1, 2026 is March 31, 2026. April 15 is 45 days after March 1. So the clause simultaneously allows 30 days and 45 days, and the difference matters if a late fee ever turns on it. Ask for the clause to state one deadline - either "within 30 days, by March 31" or "by April 15" - before signing.

Anything wrong with this invoice header?

INVOICE #4471
Date: November 31, 2026
Due: 30 days from invoice date

Can you check this school newsletter item against the student profile I was given?

Profile: "Dana R., born June 2010."
Newsletter (2020): "This week, sophomore Dana R. celebrates her 25th birthday!"

They cannot both be true. Someone born in June 2010 would have turned 10 in June 2020 - not 25. The newsletter's "25th birthday" is off by fifteen years against the profile's birth date. (The profile itself looks like the reliable half: a 10-year-old in 2020 is at least a plausible school student, while a 25-year-old sophomore with a 2010 birth date is impossible.) One of the two documents has the wrong year or the wrong age.

I'm sending this email to attendees - can you check it first?

"The workshop will be held on Wednesday, January 5, 2027, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m."

One fix before you send: January 5, 2027 is a Tuesday, not a Wednesday. Either the weekday or the date is wrong - if you mean the Wednesday, it would be January 6, 2027. Correct it now, or half your attendees will show up a day late.

Please review this venue contract's dates:

Event date: Monday, February 14, 2027
Load-in: February 30, 2027, from 8 a.m.
Event ends: February 14, 2027, at 11 p.m.

Does the term in this agreement make sense?

"Term: 24 months, commencing January 1, 2026, and ending December 31, 2028."

No - the length and the end date disagree. Twenty-four months from January 1, 2026 ends on December 31, 2027. The stated end date of December 31, 2028 is a full year later: January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2028 is 36 months, not 24. Either the term is 36 months or the end date should be in 2027, and the difference is a year of obligations, so get it corrected before signing.

Check this lease for contradictions:

Summary box: "Flexible terms - cancel anytime with no penalty."
Clause 3: "This lease automatically renews for successive twelve-month terms unless either party gives notice at least 90 days before the end of the current term."

I'm confused by my rental agreement. Section 2 says "The $800 security deposit is fully refundable within 30 days of move-out, less any deductions for damage." But Section 9 says "The deposit is non-refundable and will be retained by the landlord at the end of the term." Which is it?

On the face of the document, nobody can tell you - the two sections flatly contradict each other. Section 2 promises the $800 back (minus damage deductions) within 30 days of move-out; Section 9 says the same deposit is non-refundable and kept by the landlord regardless. Both cannot be true. Do not sign until the landlord strikes one version in writing, because whichever section survives will decide whether you ever see the $800 again.

How much notice do I have to give to end this service contract?

Clause 4: "Either party may terminate this agreement with 30 days' written notice."
Clause 11: "Termination of this agreement requires 60 days' written notice."

The contract gives two different answers. Clause 4 says 30 days' written notice; Clause 11 says 60 days. They cannot both govern, and the contract as pasted does not say which clause wins. The safe course is to plan around the longer period - 60 days - and to ask the provider, in writing, to confirm which clause applies before you rely on the 30-day version. If you give only 30 days and Clause 11 controls, you could be charged for an extra month.

Does this subscription email match its own terms?

Headline: "No commitment - cancel anytime!"
Terms below: "All plans have a 12-month minimum term. Early cancellation incurs a fee equal to the remaining months of the term."

This warranty document says in the coverage section: "This warranty covers all parts and labor for three years." Then in the exclusions it says: "Labor charges are not covered under this warranty." Am I covered for labor or not?

The document contradicts itself, so as written you cannot rely on being covered. The coverage section promises "all parts and labor for three years"; the exclusions section removes labor entirely. In practice, manufacturers usually enforce the exclusions, which would mean you pay for labor and they pay for parts - but that is a guess about their practice, not what the paper says. Get the manufacturer to confirm in writing which section governs before you authorize a repair, and keep their answer with the warranty.

Can you read this offer letter and tell me if the work arrangement is clear?

"This is a remote-first position, and you may work from anywhere.
...
You must relocate to our Austin office and work on-site five days a week within 60 days of your start date."

It is not clear - the letter promises two opposite arrangements. The first line makes the job remote-first and location-free; the later paragraph requires you to move to Austin and be in the office five days a week within 60 days of starting. Those cannot both describe the same job. Before signing, ask the employer to confirm in writing which term is real and to strike the other from the letter, because if you sign as-is, the relocation clause is the one with a deadline attached and the one they could enforce.

I have a dog - does this lease actually allow pets?

Listing summary: "Pets welcome!"
Clause 14: "No animals of any kind may be kept on the premises."

Can I pause my gym membership while I recover from surgery? The contract says in one place: "Members may pause their membership at any time for up to 3 months." But the rules section says: "Memberships cannot be suspended for any reason."

Your contract argues with itself. The membership terms expressly allow a pause of up to 3 months at any time; the rules section forbids suspension for any reason, no exceptions. Both statements are in the same document, so the honest answer is that the contract does not give you a clear right either way. Go to the gym with both passages marked, ask them to confirm the pause in writing before your surgery, and keep that confirmation - if billing disputes it later, the written confirmation plus the pause clause is much stronger than the clause alone.

What response time does this support agreement actually commit to?

SLA table: "Critical issues: first response within 4 hours."
Section 6: "We respond to all support issues within 2 business days."

For a critical issue, the agreement commits to two incompatible times. The SLA table promises a first response within 4 hours; Section 6 promises a response to all issues within 2 business days - which, over a weekend, could mean four calendar days. A critical issue cannot be governed by both. The SLA table is the more specific promise and the one written for exactly this case, but the document never says it overrides Section 6. Before signing, get the vendor to state in the agreement that the SLA table controls, or expect them to quote the 2-business-day figure when something breaks on a Friday night.

Check this insurance summary against the policy schedule:

Summary: "No deductible - we cover 100% of costs from the first dollar."
Policy schedule: "A $500 deductible applies to all claims."
This store's homepage banner says "Free returns within 60 days." Their returns page says "Items must be returned within 14 days. Return shipping is at the customer's expense." Which one applies?

The store is publishing two different policies, and they disagree on both points: the banner gives you 60 days and free returns; the returns page gives you 14 days and makes you pay the shipping. In a dispute, the store will almost certainly point to the detailed returns page, not the banner. If the generous version is part of why you're buying, take a screenshot of the banner with the date visible before you order, and consider asking the store in writing which policy is current - but plan around 14 days and paid shipping, because that is the version written like an enforceable policy.

My employment agreement says: "Employment is at-will, and either party may terminate it at any time, for any reason." But clause 8 says: "The Company shall provide six months' written notice before terminating any employee." Do those fit together?

Not as written. At-will employment means the company can end the relationship at any time - including today, with no notice required. Clause 8 obliges the company to give six months' written notice before any termination. An employer cannot simultaneously be free to terminate at any moment and be required to give half a year's notice first. One of the two clauses has to yield, and the agreement doesn't say which. This is worth raising with the employer (or an employment lawyer) before signing, because the difference between the two readings is six months of pay.

We're expecting about 180 guests. Does this venue contract work for us?

Introduction: "Our grand hall accommodates up to 200 guests for seated events."
Clause 19 (fire safety): "Maximum occupancy for the grand hall is 120 persons, including staff and vendors."

The summary page of this loan says: "Your rate is fixed for the life of the loan - it will never change." The disclosure booklet says: "After the third year, the interest rate adjusts annually based on the published index plus a margin." Is my rate fixed or not?

According to these two pages, both - which means the documents contradict each other on the single most important term of the loan. A rate that is fixed for life cannot start adjusting annually after year three. The product described in the disclosure (fixed for three years, then adjustable) is a known loan type, and the summary page appears to describe a different one. Do not sign until the lender corrects the summary in writing and confirms which structure you are actually getting; over a long loan, the difference between the two is measured in tens of thousands of dollars.

The sales email for this software says: "Buy once - this is a perpetual license, yours forever." But the license terms say: "This license expires 12 months after the date of purchase." What am I actually buying?

On paper, you're being sold two different products. The email offers a perpetual license that never expires; the license terms grant you 12 months. "Perpetual" and "expires in a year" cannot both be true. The license terms are the document that governs the software's activation, so expect the program to stop working after 12 months unless the vendor confirms the perpetual license in writing. Ask them to reconcile the two before you pay - a one-line email from the vendor saying the license is perpetual would settle it.

What do I need to provide for this cleaning service?

Agreement: "We bring all supplies and equipment needed for each visit."
Client checklist: "Before each visit, please provide a vacuum cleaner and all cleaning products."

Check this apartment listing for consistency:

Headline: "Spacious 1,200 sq ft 2-bedroom!"
Floor plan details: "Total living area: 950 sq ft. Bedroom 1: 12x14. Bedroom 2: 11x13."

Does this offer letter's pay band make sense?

"The compensation band for this role is $85,000-$80,000. Your offer of $82,000 sits within the band."

No - the band is written backwards. A range of "$85,000-$80,000" has its top below its bottom, so as written the band is empty and no salary can sit "within" it. The offer of $82,000 falls between the two numbers, which suggests the band was simply typed in reverse (probably $80,000-$85,000) - but get the letter corrected, because as signed, the document promises a pay band that cannot exist.

This house listing says "3 bed / 2 bath" at the top, but the description says "Both bedrooms are generously sized, and the main bathroom was renovated in 2024." The floor plan labels Bedroom 1 and Bedroom 2. Is it a 3-bed or not?

On the listing's own evidence, it is a 2-bedroom house being advertised as 3. The description says "both bedrooms," and the floor plan labels only Bedroom 1 and Bedroom 2 - neither mentions a third bedroom anywhere. Unless there is a third room the listing simply never describes, the headline figure is wrong. Ask the agent directly where the third bedroom is; if the answer is a converted den or garage, that also matters for how the house is valued and permitted.

Check this car listing:

Headline: "Only 42,000 miles - barely driven!"
Service history (from the same listing): "Last serviced at 58,300 miles, odometer reading recorded by dealer, March 2026."
This laptop's product page headline says "20-hour battery life!" but the spec table at the bottom says "Battery life: up to 11 hours." Which should I believe?

Believe the spec table, and treat the headline as a red flag. The page contradicts itself by nearly a factor of two: 20 hours in the headline, 11 hours in the detailed specifications. Spec tables are usually generated from the manufacturer's data sheet, while headlines are marketing copy - and "up to 11 hours" is itself the best-case figure. Plan around 11 hours or less, and consider asking the seller why the headline doubles their own specification.

This vacation rental looks great. The photo caption says "Your private pool - included with every stay!" But the terms at the bottom say "Pool access is not included in the rental rate. Community pool passes are available at the front desk for $25 per day." Which is true?

Neither, cleanly - the listing promises one thing in the caption and the opposite in its terms. The caption advertises a "private pool, included with every stay"; the terms say pool access is not included at all, and the pool you can actually use is a shared community pool at $25 a day. So on the listing's own words, the pool is neither private nor included. If the pool matters to your trip, message the host and get the real arrangement in writing before booking.

Does this job posting contradict itself?

Banner: "No experience required - we train the right person!"
Requirements section: "Minimum 5 years of experience in a similar role is required."
This event page says "FREE ADMISSION for all!" in big letters at the top, but the details section says "Tickets: $15 at the door, cash or card." Is admission free or not?

Yes - the page contradicts its own headline. The details section says: "Tickets: $15 at the door, cash or card." So admission is not free; it costs $15. The headline and the details cannot both be right. Budget for the $15, and if free admission was announced anywhere else (a poster, a social post), it is worth a quick message to the organizer - either the price or the headline is a mistake they will want to fix before the event.
I'm about to buy this table from a listing titled "Solid Oak Dining Table." The materials line says "Oak veneer over an engineered particleboard core." Is that the same thing?

No - and that difference is exactly why the listing is misleading. "Solid oak" means the table is made of oak timber throughout. Veneer over particleboard means a thin layer of oak on the surface with compressed wood-chip board underneath - a different material, with different weight, durability, repairability, and value. The title and the materials line describe two different products. If you still want it, price it as a veneer table, not a solid oak one, and don't pay a solid-oak price.

We're hoping to move fast - check this listing:

"Available March 1 - move in right away!"
Lease details: "Current tenant in place through April 30. Earliest move-in date: May 1."
This course page says "A 6-week course - one live session per week." But the schedule underneath lists sessions in Week 1, Week 2, all the way through Week 10. How long is the course?

The page gives two incompatible answers. The description promises 6 weeks at one session per week, which would be 6 sessions. The schedule lists 10 weekly sessions, which is a 10-week course. One of them is wrong by four weeks - a real difference if you're planning around an end date or comparing the price per session. Ask the provider which is correct before enrolling; if the schedule is right, you're committing to nearly twice the calendar time the headline suggests.

This phone plan advertises "UNLIMITED DATA - no caps, ever." The fine print says: "Data usage above 50 GB per billing cycle will be throttled to 128 kbps for the remainder of the cycle." Is it really unlimited?

Yes, and it directly contradicts the headline. The plan's fine print says: "Data usage above 50 GB per billing cycle will be throttled to 128 kbps for the remainder of the cycle." A 50 GB cap with throttling after it is, by definition, not "unlimited data with no caps." In fairness, 50 GB is generous for most people and 128 kbps still passes messages - but if you regularly use more than 50 GB, the plan you actually get is very different from the plan in the headline.

We're a group of six looking at this cabin:

"Sleeps 6 comfortably!"
Bedrooms: "Two twin beds in the loft and one double bed in the main bedroom."

Can you check the start date in this offer letter? It says "Your start date is Monday, June 1, 2026." But the last paragraph says "Please arrive at 9 a.m. on your first day, Monday, June 8, 2026." Both are Mondays, so...?

You've spotted it exactly - and the fact that both dates really are Mondays in June 2026 is what makes the trap easy to miss. June 1 and June 8 are both Mondays, a week apart, and the letter names each one as your first day. They can't both be your start date. Nothing else in the letter resolves it, so ask HR in writing which Monday is your actual first day before you give notice or book anything around either date - showing up a week early is awkward, but showing up a week late looks like a no-show.

Check this flight booking before I pay:

Flight 1: Arrives Denver 2:05 p.m.
Flight 2: Departs Denver 2:30 p.m.
Note in the booking: "Minimum connection time at Denver International: 45 minutes."

Does this hotel confirmation look right?

Check-in: March 12, 2026
Check-out: March 10, 2026
Length of stay: 3 nights

No - it has the stay running backwards. Check-out (March 10) is two days before check-in (March 12), which would make the stay negative two nights, not three. For a 3-night stay starting March 12, check-out should be March 15. One of the dates is a typo, and since the "3 nights" agrees with a March 12 start, the check-out date is the likely error. Get the hotel to reissue the confirmation before you travel - an unreconciled confirmation is how people arrive to find their room released.

Can you spot anything wrong with this trip itinerary?

Outbound: Arrive Honolulu December 30
Return: Flight departs Honolulu December 28

Yes - the trip ends before it begins. The return flight leaves Honolulu on December 28, two days before you arrive there on December 30. One of the dates is wrong (a return in early January would make sense for a December 30 arrival). Fix it with the airline now, because as booked, the return leg is unusable.

Check this train ticket:

Departs: 9:15 a.m.
Arrives: 8:50 a.m. (same day)
Journey time: 2 hours 35 minutes

Check my car rental confirmation:

Pick-up: Friday, June 12, 2026, 10:00 a.m.
Return: Thursday, June 11, 2026, 10:00 a.m.
Rental period: 7 days

It contradicts itself twice. First, the return (Thursday, June 11) is the day before the pick-up (Friday, June 12) - you would be returning the car before collecting it. Second, neither reading gives a 7-day rental: June 11 to June 12 is one day. A genuine 7-day rental picked up on Friday, June 12 would be due back Friday, June 19. Call the rental company and have the confirmation reissued with dates that agree with each other and with the 7 days you're paying for.

Does this tour itinerary flow properly?

Day 1 - June 11: Arrive in Lisbon, walking tour
Day 2 - June 12: Sintra day trip
Day 3 - June 14: Porto by train
Day 4 - June 13: Douro Valley cruise

Almost - the last two days run backwards. Day 3 is dated June 14 and Day 4 is dated June 13, so the itinerary has you in Porto on the 14th and then cruising the Douro on the 13th, the day before. Days 1 and 2 (June 11 and 12) are in order, so it's just the Day 3/Day 4 dates that are swapped or mistyped. Ask the operator which date belongs to which activity before you book anything around them, like the Porto train.

Is there a problem with this booking confirmation?

Flight: Lands 11:40 p.m.
Hotel note: "Reception closes at 10:00 p.m. Late check-in is not possible. Rooms not claimed by closing time are released."

Check the timing on this cruise day, please:

Ship arrives in port: 8:00 a.m.
Shore excursion departs from the port: 7:30 a.m. (same day)

The excursion leaves before you get there. It departs the port at 7:30 a.m., but your ship doesn't arrive until 8:00 a.m. - a 30-minute gap in the wrong direction, and that's before any time for disembarking. Either the excursion time or the arrival time in the itinerary is wrong. Raise it with the cruise line now; if the 8:00 arrival is right, you need a later excursion or a refund for this one.
The booking site describes this as "Your 5-day trip: March 3 - March 10, 2026." Is that 5 days?

No. March 3 to March 10, 2026 is 7 nights - 8 calendar days inclusive. A 5-day trip starting March 3 would end on March 7 (or run 5 nights to March 8, depending on how they count). The label and the dates disagree by about two days, which matters if the price, the hotel nights, or your time off were calculated from "5 days." Check what you're actually being charged for before paying.

Can you check this conference travel email for problems?

"Your workshop ends at 5:00 p.m. Your airport shuttle departs the venue at 4:30 p.m. Your flight departs at 6:00 p.m. - please arrive at the airport 90 minutes before departure."
Hotel confirmation says: "4 nights - check-in June 10, 2026, check-out June 13, 2026." We're being charged for 4 nights. Is that right?

No - the dates describe 3 nights, not 4. June 10 to June 13 is three nights (the 10th, 11th, and 12th), with check-out on the morning of the 13th. Four nights from June 10 would check out on June 14. So either the check-out date is wrong or you're being charged for a night that isn't in the booking. Ask the hotel to reconcile the dates with the charge before you pay.
This flight email says: "Departs 10:00 a.m., arrives 1:30 p.m. All times local; both cities are in the same time zone. Flight duration: 2 hours 10 minutes." Does that hang together?

No. With both cities in the same time zone - as the email itself states - 10:00 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. is 3 hours 30 minutes in the air, not 2 hours 10 minutes. The stated duration is 1 hour 20 minutes shorter than the stated times allow. One of the three figures (departure, arrival, or duration) is wrong. It matters practically: if the 1:30 arrival is the typo and you really land at 12:10, any pickup or connection planned around 1:30 still works - but if the duration is the typo, plan for the later landing. Confirm with the airline.

Check this annual report summary against its own table:

Executive summary: "Revenue grew 8% this year, continuing our expansion."
Table: 2025 revenue: $1.25M. 2026 revenue: $1.15M.
Our survey report says: "How do you commute to work? (Choose one) Drive: 45%. Public transit: 35%. Bike or walk: 28%." A reader says the numbers can't be right. Are they?

Your reader is correct. Because the question says "choose one," the three shares must add to 100% - but 45 + 35 + 28 = 108%. Eight percentage points too many. Either one of the figures is mistyped, or the percentages were computed against different bases and pasted together. (If the question had allowed multiple answers, a total over 100% would be fine - but as written, it doesn't.) Recalculate from the raw counts before the report circulates.

Can you check this study summary for consistency?

Methods: "We surveyed 240 customers over two weeks."
Results: "Of the 320 respondents, 61% said they would recommend us."

The sample size changes between sections. Methods says 240 customers were surveyed; Results reports on 320 respondents.
